title: A letter from Sapporo
text:
14 Ginkgo Street
Sapporo, Hokkaido
Japan

18 November

Dear Citra,

Thank you for your last letter and the photograph of the Bogor rain. I laughed when you wrote that your town is nicknamed the Rain City, because you looked so cheerful standing in the middle of it with your umbrella upside down! I showed the photo to my whole class, and everyone wanted to know whether the rain is warm. When I said that you told me it is, they all went quiet and looked jealous.

I have exciting news of my own. The first snow arrived last Thursday. I was in the middle of a maths lesson when somebody whispered "Yuki da!", which means "It's snowing!" Nobody listened to the teacher after that. Twenty-eight faces turned towards the window, and Mr Tanaka, who has seen the first snow of the year about forty times, smiled and let us watch for a full minute.

Funnily enough, my name, Yuki, actually means snow, so my friends always tease me at this time of year. They say I am responsible for it.

Now the town is changing. The snowploughs rumble through the streets before dawn, and we wear thick boots to school with spikes on the soles so we do not slip. Mum lays a mat inside the front door for our wet shoes. The schoolyard is already soft and white, and at break we build tiny snowmen along the fence, because there is not enough snow yet for big ones.

In February our city holds a huge snow festival, with giant sculptures made of ice and snow as tall as houses. Last year I helped to build a snow rabbit with my cousins. It took us three whole afternoons and it was the size of a car. I have attached a drawing of it, though my drawing is not very good!

I have never seen a real mango tree, but I think about the ones in your letters. Do you pick them yourself? Is it true that you can eat them with chilli and salt? I would be brave enough to try, I think.

Please write soon and tell me what the rainy season smells like. I have always wondered.

Your friend,

Yuki
